chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
The financing of an income property follows different rules from those of a house. Down payment, taking into account rents, loan insurance: well planned, your financing can make or break the profitability of your project.

This guide covers the main rules (1 to 4 homes vs. 5 and more), the contribution, the role of loan insurance programs and the importance of good planning.

2026 edition note: rules and rates are changing; always confirm with a mortgage broker. Each chapter ends with a lined “My Notes” page.

Financing an income property does not follow the same rules as a residence. This guide clarifies the distinction 1-4 vs 5+ homes, the down payment, the role of loan insurers and how the lender qualifies your file.

Objective: set up solid financing that protects your profitability, rather than chasing the lowest rate.

chapters.title: 1 to 4 dwellings vs 5 dwellings and more
chapters.objective: Understanding the key dividing line in rental financing.
chapters.html:
Understand the key dividing line in rental financing.

The fundamental distinction: buildings with 1 to 4 housing units are financed according to rules close to residential, while buildings with 5 housing units and more are considered “commercial” (multiple housing units), with different rules, capital outlay and analysis, focused on the profitability of the building.

  • 1 to 4 homes: lower down payment, especially if you occupy a home.
  • 5 units and more: higher down payment, analysis based on the building's RNE.
  • The border of the 5 dwellings changes your setup a lot.

The key dividing line: 1 to 4 dwellings (rules close to residential, lower down payment if you occupy) vs 5 dwellings and more (commercial financing, higher down payment, analysis based on the income of the building). This distinction changes your entire edit.

Emilie's advice

The move from 4 to 5 housing units changes everything in terms of financing. If you're just starting out, a building with 4 units or less is often the most accessible entry point.

chapters.title: Down payment and occupancy
chapters.objective: Optimize the contribution according to your project.
chapters.html:
Optimize the contribution according to your project.

For a building of 1 to 4 units that you occupy, the down payment can be significantly reduced (see the owner-occupant guide). For an unoccupied rental property, the required contribution is generally higher.

  • Occupant (1-4 dwellings): reduced contribution, better conditions.
  • Non-occupying investor: greater contribution.
  • A portion of the rent can help qualify your loan.

Optimize your contribution according to your project: occupying a 1-4 unit accommodation opens up advantageous rules; a purely rental property requires more. The lender also retains a portion of the rent in your capacity - a lever to be calculated precisely.

Emilie's advice

If your situation allows it, occupying accommodation in your first plex unlocks much more advantageous financing. This is often the best springboard to start.

chapters.title: Loan insurance and taking into account rents
chapters.objective: Understand the role of insurance programs.
chapters.html:
Understand the role of insurance programs.

Loan insurers (CMHC and others) offer multi-housing programs that can allow for a reduced down payment and better conditions, for a premium. The rents of the building are taken into account in the analysis, to varying degrees.

These programs and their criteria are evolving: a mortgage broker specializing in income properties is your best ally in identifying the best option.

Loan insurers (CMHC and others) offer programs that can reduce the down payment or improve the conditions, particularly for rentals. They take into account rents according to precise rules. A specialized mortgage broker knows these programs and their criteria.

Emilie's advice

Work with a mortgage broker familiar with rentals. The right insurance program or lender can turn a borderline project into a profitable one.

chapters.title: Build a solid assembly
chapters.html:
Assemble financing that protects profitability.

  • Compare several lenders (rates AND conditions, penalties, flexibility).
  • Provide a margin: if rates rise at renewal, does the project hold up?
  • Keep cash for unforeseen events and work.
  • Think about what’s next: a good arrangement makes the next purchase (refinancing) easier.

Financing is not just a formality: it is a strategic lever that determines your cash flow and your ability to grow.

A solid arrangement compares several lenders (rates AND conditions), provides a reserve, and does not bet everything on an optimistic scenario. The best rate with rigid conditions can be expensive at the wrong time: think penalties, portability and accelerated repayments.

Emilie's advice

Don't just choose the lowest rate: think about flexibility and the ability to refinance. Your first montage should open the door to the second building.

chapters.title: Qualification: ratios and stress test
chapters.objective: Understand how the lender rates you.
chapters.html:
Understand how the lender evaluates you.

Obtaining financing depends on how the lender evaluates your file :

  • Debt ratios : proportion of your income devoted to debts.
  • Taking into account rents : only part is often retained.
  • Resistance test : your capacity is calculated at a rate higher than the actual rate, to verify that you would sustain an increase.

Knowing these rules in advance avoids refusals and helps you build a solid case.

The lender evaluates you via debt ratios, partial consideration of rents, and a stress test (qualification at a higher rate). Knowing these rules in advance avoids refusals: meet a broker specializing in rentals BEFORE shopping.

Emilie's advice

Meet a mortgage broker specializing in rental real estate BEFORE you shop. It will tell you exactly how much you can borrow and how rents are taken into account - it targets your searches.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, concretely.

This week

  1. Determine the number of accommodations and my status (occupant or not).
  2. Meet a mortgage broker specializing in rentals.

Within 30 days

  1. Compare programs and lenders (rates and conditions).
  2. Structure a package with a margin for rate increases.

Then

  1. Secure financing that protects cash flow and growth.

Before you shop

  1. Meet a mortgage broker specializing in rental real estate.
  2. Have my capacity calculated (rent included) and compare rates AND conditions.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• 1-4 housing units: financing regime close to residential.
  • 5 dwellings and more: “commercial” multi-dwelling, analysis by the RNE.
  • Contribution / capital outlay: lower if occupant, higher if pure investor.
  • Multi-housing loan insurance: programs (CMHC, etc.) with reduced contribution, with premium.
  • Refinancing: leverage to finance the next purchase.
  • 1-4 housing units: category close to residential, more flexible financing.
  • 5 homes and more: commercial financing, based on income.
  • Loan insurance: program reducing the down payment or improving the conditions.
  • Strength test: qualification at a rate higher than the actual rate.
  • Taking into account rents: share of income retained by the lender.
